choices.why: Perfect participle of καταμφιέννυμι, 'clothe': the image of the grain's covering.

choices.english: the one who speaks for God

choices.why: εἰσκρίνω, bring in: the new things that replace the old.

pass_a_gloss: [Completing the grain simile of the previous section: in a covering of body and with an addition] of beauty, springing up (ἀναφύω), is marvelled at, in this same very manner the human body too is sown in corruption and in weakness and in dishonour, but will live again clothed (καταμφιέννυμι) in honour and incorruption and indeed also power. And it is worth marvelling at the sobriety (νῆψις) of the God-speaker (θεηγόρος); for having the faith firmly set (ἐρείδω), and trusting that it will live again in every way and altogether, he likens (παρεικάζω) the corruption of the body to sowing, very skilfully and wisely making the nature of the thing like the example in every respect. Therefore, like the grain, the body will not live again bare, he says, but very well covered round (περιστέλλω) with incorruption and glory, and besides these the strength (εὐσθενές), and indeed being enriched also with this, to be in a spiritual mind (φρόνημα), the grace from above and the incomparable power of the Maker of all re-forming in a certain manner the things in it toward the whole opposite. For there are present in the fallen body, sown as it were into earth, corruption and weakness and the unlovely (ἀκαλλής), and the natural (ψυχικός) mind, which we say is the same as the fleshly and more earthy (γεώδης); but since it was brought forth to coming-to-be in the beginnings not being so by nature, and these things slipped in (παρεισδύω) through the transgression and the penalty upon death, our nature calling us back (ἀναφωνέω) to what was in the beginnings, the putting away (ἀπόθεσις) of the things thrown in between (παρεισβάλλω) is done of necessity by the power and working of God, and in exchange is brought in (ἀντεισκρίνω) the participation (μέθεξις) of the goods that were first and in the beginnings in us. For we have been renewed (ἀνακαινίζω) in Christ according to the Scriptures; for a holy prophet said, 'Be bold, Zion, let your hands not be slackened (παρίημι); the Lord your God is in you, powerful to save you, and he will renew you in his loving.' For when the God and Father loved us, then, then also he renewed us in Christ; and indeed it is true that all things in him are 'a new creation; and the ancient things passed by, and new things have come to be.' And what ancient things does he mean? The things that have ridden past (παριππεύω). And what new? The things brought in (εἰσκρίνω). Old the corruption, and indeed the feebleness (ἄναλκις), and besides this the ill-fame (δυσκλεής), and the charges (ἔγκλημα) of the natural mind; and new through Christ, glory and incorruption and power and the spiritual mind; for our body will be spiritual. What would the spiritual be, O initiator (μυσταγωγός)? Will it then be flesh no longer, and be in no way compounded (σύγκειμαι), as of course even now, of bones and sinews, through which the nature of the body according to us would be completed; but will it rather be thin (ἰσχνός) and air-like (ἀερώδης) and yielding little to shadows, he says? Not at all; for if some suppose these things to hold so, surely it will not be the very thing falling into earth that will live again, but something other beside that, and in no way resembling the first. And I would say that spiritual is not the thing in the form of a shadow, or of a bodiless spirit, but rather the thing that has stood away (ἀφίστημι) and indeed been wholly freed (ἀπαλλάσσω) from the fleshly and more earthy mind. [Lemma] For if there is, he says, a natural body, there is also [continued in the next section].
pass_b_english: …beauty, and is admired, so in this same way the human body too is sown in corruption, in weakness and in dishonor, but will come back to life clothed in honor and incorruption, and in power as well (1 Corinthians 15:42–43).

The sober watchfulness of the one who speaks for God deserves our admiration. For his faith is firmly grounded, and he is confident that the body will come back to life in every way and without fail; so he likens the body's corruption to sowing, and with great skill and wisdom makes the nature of the thing match the example at every point. So, he says, like the grain, the body will not come back to life bare, but richly clothed with incorruption and glory, and with strength besides, and enriched also with this: that it comes to be of a spiritual mind, since the grace from above and the incomparable power of the Creator of all in a way refashion what is in it into the very opposite.

For corruption and weakness and lack of beauty dwell in the body that has fallen and been sown, as it were, in the earth, and a natural mind as well, which we say is the same as the fleshly and more earthly mind. But it was not so by nature when it was brought into being in the beginning; these things crept in through the transgression and the sentence of death. Since our nature is being called back to what it was in the beginning, the putting off of what came in between is necessarily brought about by the power and working of God, and in exchange there is brought in a share in the good things that were ours first, in the beginning.

For we have been renewed in Christ, as the Scriptures say. A holy prophet said, “Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands grow slack. The Lord your God is in you, mighty to save you, and He will renew you in His love” (Zephaniah 3:16–17). For when God the Father loved us, then, at that very time, He renewed us in Christ. And indeed it is true that all things in Him are “a new creation; the old things have passed away, and new things have come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

What old things does he mean? Those that have gone by. And what new things? Those that have been brought in. The old are corruption, and weakness, and dishonor besides, and the faults of the natural mind; the new, through Christ, are glory and incorruption and power and the spiritual mind. For our body will be spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44).

What would “spiritual” mean, O teacher of the mysteries? Does he mean that it will no longer be flesh, and will in no way be composed, as it is now, of bones and sinews, through which the nature of our body is made complete, but will rather be thin and airy, hardly more solid than a shadow? Not at all. For if some think this is how things stand, then surely it will not be the very thing that falls into the earth that comes back to life, but something else beside it, in no way like the first.

I would say that “spiritual” means not what has the form of a shadow, that is, of a bodiless spirit, but rather what has stood apart from, and indeed been wholly set free from, the fleshly and more earthly mind. “For if there is,” he says, “a natural body, there is also…
